claim: Hedgehog (Hh) morphogens are dually lipidated 19 kDa proteins that are firmly anchored to the cell membrane of producing cells.
source: Hedgehog (Hh) morphogens are dually lipidated 19 kDa proteins that are firmly anchored to the cell membrane of producing cells.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the introduction describing the biochemical properties of Hh proteins.

claim: Production of all active Hhs begins with autocatalytic cleavage of a precursor molecule by its C-terminal cholesterol transferase domain (Porter et al., 1996b).
source: Production of all active Hhs begins with autocatalytic cleavage of a precursor molecule by its C-terminal cholesterol transferase domain (Porter et al., 1996b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Porter et al., 1996b.

claim: Autocatalytic cleavage results in cholesteroylated vertebrate Sonic hedgehog (Shh) and Drosophila Hh.
source: This results in cholesteroylated vertebrate Sonic hedgehog (Shh) and Drosophila Hh.
evidence: This follows from the previous statement about autocatalytic cleavage and is presented as established knowledge.

claim: Hh acyltransferase (Hhat, also designated Skinny hedgehog or Raspberry) attaches a palmitoyl group to a conserved N-terminal cysteine that becomes exposed after signal peptide cleavage (Chamoun et al., 2001; Lee and Treisman, 2001; Micchelli et al., 2002).
source: Next, Hh acyltransferase (Hhat, also designated Skinny hedgehog or Raspberry) attaches a palmitoyl group to a conserved N-terminal cysteine that becomes exposed after signal peptide cleavage (Chamoun et al., 2001; Lee and Treisman, 2001; Micchelli et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by three citations.

claim: Hh palmitoylation is critical for later signaling, demonstrated by mutation of the N-terminal cysteine to serine or alanine (C25 > A/S in ShhC25A/S, C85 >A/S in Drosophila HhC85A/S) which abolishes palmitoylation and results in morphogen inactivity (Chamoun et al., 2001; Chen et al., 2004; Dawber et al., 2005; Goetz et al., 2006; Kohtz et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2001; Pepinsky et al., 1998).
source: Hh palmitoylation is critical for later signaling, demonstrated by mutation of the N-terminal cysteine to serine or alanine (C25 > A/S in ShhC25A/S, C85 >A/S in Drosophila HhC85A/S) which abolishes palmitoylation and results in morphogen inactivity (Chamoun et al., 2001; Chen et al., 2004; Dawber et al., 2005; Goetz et al., 2006; Kohtz et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2001; Pepinsky et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations describing experimental evidence.

claim: All Hhs multimerize at the surface of producing cells which requires binding to the long, unbranched heparan sulfate (HS) chains of cell surface HS proteoglycans (HSPGs) called glypicans (Chang et al., 2011; Ortmann et al., 2015; Vyas et al., 2008).
source: Another unusual feature of all Hhs is their multimerization at the surface of producing cells which requires binding to the long, unbranched heparan sulfate (HS) chains of cell surface HS proteoglycans (HSPGs) called glypicans (Chang et al., 2011; Ortmann et al., 2015; Vyas et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by three citations.

claim: The Hh cholesterol modification is sufficient to drive multimerization (Feng et al., 2004; Gallet et al., 2006; Koleva et al., 2015; Ohlig et al., 2011).
source: The Hh cholesterol modification is sufficient to drive this process (Feng et al., 2004; Gallet et al., 2006; Koleva et al., 2015; Ohlig et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by four citations.

claim: Multimeric Hhs initiate the Hh response in distant cells that express the Hh receptor Patched (Ptc).
source: Despite membrane anchorage and cell-surface HS association, the multimeric Hhs initiate the Hh response in distant cells that express the Hh receptor Patched (Ptc).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Hh signaling.

claim: Current models propose lipidated Hh transport on filopodia called cytonemes (Bischoff et al., 2013; Sanders et al., 2013).
source: The most current models propose lipidated Hh transport on filopodia called cytonemes (Bischoff et al., 2013; Sanders et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by two citations describing proposed transport mechanisms.

claim: Current models propose lipidated Hh transport on secreted vesicles called exosomes (Gradilla et al., 2014).
source: or on secreted vesicles called exosomes (Gradilla et al., 2014) to bridge the distance between Hh-producing and receiving cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation describing an alternative transport mechanism.

claim: In vitro, membrane-proximal shedding releases Hh ectodomains from their lipidated N-terminal peptides (Dierker et al., 2009; Ohlig et al., 2011).
source: In vitro, membrane-proximal shedding not only releases Hh ectodomains from their lipidated N-terminal peptides (Dierker et al., 2009; Ohlig et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by two citations describing in vitro experiments.

claim: N-terminal lipidated peptides block adjacent Hh-binding sites for the receptor Ptc and thereby render Hh at the cell membrane inactive.
source: This is because N-terminal lipidated peptides block adjacent Hh-binding sites for the receptor Ptc and, thereby, render Hh at the cell membrane inactive.
evidence: This is presented as a mechanistic explanation based on previous work.

claim: Sheddases unmask Ptc binding sites of solubilized clusters by cleaving inhibitory peptides during release and thereby couple Hh solubilization with its bioactivation.
source: By cleaving these inhibitory peptides during release, sheddases unmask Ptc binding sites of solubilized clusters and thereby couple Hh solubilization with its bioactivation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model based on the previous observations.

claim: The N-palmitate ensures reliable membrane-proximal positioning of inhibitory N-terminal peptides as a prerequisite for their efficient proteolytic processing.
source: In this model, the N-palmitate plays two indirect roles for Hh biofunction: first, it ensures reliable membrane-proximal positioning of inhibitory N-terminal peptides as a prerequisite for their efficient proteolytic processing
evidence: This is a proposed mechanistic role based on the model.

claim: The N-palmitate ensures that only fully processed (=activated) Hh clusters are released by its continued association with the cell membrane.
source: and second, by its continued association with the cell membrane, it ensures that only fully processed (=activated) Hh clusters are released.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanistic role based on the model.

claim: Inhibition of N-palmitoylation will result in release of inactive soluble proteins with masked Ptc-binding sites (Jakobs et al., 2014; Jakobs et al., 2016; Ohlig et al., 2011; Ohlig et al., 2012).
source: This model therefore predicts that inhibition of N-palmitoylation will result in release of inactive soluble proteins with masked Ptc-binding sites (Jakobs et al., 2014; Jakobs et al., 2016; Ohlig et al., 2011; Ohlig et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model supported by citations.

claim: Impaired or delayed processing of dual-lipidated Hh will strongly reduce its release and bioactivity in vivo.
source: It also predicts that impaired or delayed processing of dual-lipidated Hh will strongly reduce its release and bioactivity in vivo.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: Non-palmitoylated HhC85S has a dominant negative, cell-autonomous function in endogenous Hh.
source: By uncovering a dominant negative, cell-autonomous function of non-palmitoylated HhC85S in endogenous Hh, we here support the first prediction.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: Hh clusters form by direct protein-protein contact.
source: we provide strong evidence that Hh clusters form by direct protein-protein contact
evidence: This is a conclusion from the current study based on experimental evidence.

claim: Unprocessed N-terminal peptides block Ptc binding of adjacent endogenous Hhs.
source: and that unprocessed N-terminal peptides block Ptc binding of adjacent endogenous Hhs.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the current study based on experimental evidence.

claim: Soluble clusters with masked Ptc-binding sites impair direct patterning of the 3–4 intervein region of the wing due to their reduced activity.
source: As a consequence, we suggest that, due to their reduced activity, soluble clusters with masked Ptc-binding sites impair direct patterning of the 3–4 intervein region of the wing.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the current study based on experimental evidence.

claim: Targeted deletion of non-palmitoylated inhibitory peptides restores 3–4 intervein formation.
source: Supporting this mechanism, targeted deletion on non-palmitoylated inhibitory peptides restores 3–4 intervein formation.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: Impaired or delayed processing of lipidated Hh strongly reduces its solubilization and bioactivity in vivo.
source: We also show that impaired or delayed processing of lipidated Hh strongly reduces its solubilization, and hence its bioactivity, in vivo.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: The HS-binding Cardin-Weintraub (CW) motif serves as the preferred N-terminal Hh processing site in vivo.
source: We demonstrate that the HS-binding Cardin-Weintraub (CW) motif serves as the preferred N-terminal Hh processing site in vivo
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: Impaired processing of the CW site completely abolishes direct 3–4 intervein wing patterning.
source: and that impaired processing of this site completely abolishes direct 3–4 intervein wing patterning.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: Additional targeted deletion of N-palmitate restores wing patterning when CW site processing is impaired.
source: Additional targeted deletion of N-palmitate restores wing patterning, demonstrating that one role of palmitoylated membrane anchors is to prevent the release of un- or incompletely processed Hh clusters in vivo.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: One role of palmitoylated membrane anchors is to prevent the release of un- or incompletely processed Hh clusters in vivo.
source: demonstrating that one role of palmitoylated membrane anchors is to prevent the release of un- or incompletely processed Hh clusters in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the current study based on experimental evidence.

claim: Shh forms variably sized cell surface clusters, with the largest complexes exceeding sizes of 100 nm.
source: Three α-Shh antibodies detected Shh in variably sized cell surface clusters, with the largest complexes exceeding sizes of 100 nm.
evidence: This is based on immunoelectron microscopy analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Many Shh clusters consisted of linear arrangements or contained linear arrays of closely packed gold particles.
source: Notably, as shown in Figure 1a–h and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, many clusters consisted of linear arrangements (Figure 1a–d) or contained linear arrays of closely packed gold particles (Figure 1f,g, arrowheads).
evidence: This is based on immunoelectron microscopy analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Nearest-neighbour analysis of the angular distribution between the three most proximal gold particles confirmed that most arrangements were rectangular (90°) or linear (180°).
source: Nearest-neighbour analysis of the angular distribution between the three most proximal gold particles (Figure 1i) confirmed that most arrangements were rectangular (90°) or linear (180°)
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of immunoelectron microscopy data shown in Figure 1i.

claim: Linear Hh arrangements are consistent with Hh multimerization using linear HS chains of glypican HSPGs as templates (Chang et al., 2011; Vyas et al., 2008; Schuermann et al., 2018).
source: the latter being consistent with Hh multimerization using linear HS chains of glypican HSPGs as templates (Chang et al., 2011; Vyas et al., 2008; Schuermann et al., 2018).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Hh linearization during cell-surface multimerization is consistent with a zig-zag arrangement of Hh monomers.
source: Hh linearization during cell-surface multimerization is further consistent with previous structural and biochemical data which suggest a zig-zag arrangement of Hh monomers (Figure 1j)
evidence: This is based on structural modeling shown in Figure 1j and previous data.

claim: Drosophila Hh and vertebrate Shh form variably sized clusters ranging from 80 kDa to 600 kDa (Chang et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2004; Jakobs et al., 2014; Ohlig et al., 2011; Ohlig et al., 2012).
source: and variably sized Drosophila Hh and vertebrate Shh, ranging from 80 kDa to 600 kDa (Chang et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2004; Jakobs et al., 2014; Ohlig et al., 2011; Ohlig et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous biochemical studies.

claim: The fly wing develops from the imaginal wing disc.
source: The fly wing develops from the imaginal wing disc (Figure 2a, bottom).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila development, illustrated in Figure 2a.

claim: The wing primordium at the center of the wing disc differentiates into the wing blade proper, which shows a characteristic pattern of five longitudinal veins (L1-5), an anterior cross vein (connecting L3 and L4) and a posterior cross vein (connecting L4 and L5) (Hartl and Scott, 2014).
source: The wing primordium at the center of the wing disc differentiates into the wing blade proper, which shows a characteristic pattern of five longitudinal veins (L1-5), an anterior cross vein (connecting L3 and L4) and a posterior cross vein (connecting L4 and L5) (Figure 2a, top) (Hartl and Scott, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila wing development, supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 2a.

claim: The anterior/posterior (a/p) boundary is located slightly anterior to the position of L4 in the adult wing.
source: The anterior/posterior (a/p) boundary is located slightly anterior to the position of L4 in the adult wing (Figure 2a, red dashed line).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila wing anatomy, illustrated in Figure 2a.

claim: Hh is produced in the posterior wing disc compartment under the control of the transcription factor Engrailed (en) (Tabata et al., 1992; Zecca et al., 1995).
source: Hh is produced in the posterior wing disc compartment under the control of the transcription factor Engrailed (en) (Tabata et al., 1992; Zecca et al., 1995)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by two citations.

claim: Engrailed acts indirectly on Hh expression through the repression of the transcriptional Hh repressor Cubitus interruptus (Ci) (Bejarano and Milán, 2009).
source: which acts indirectly on Hh expression through the repression of the transcriptional Hh repressor Cubitus interruptus (Ci) (Bejarano and Milán, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Hh moves across the a/p boundary into the anterior compartment, where it binds to Ptc (Ingham et al., 1991).
source: Hh then moves across the a/p boundary into the anterior compartment, where it binds to Ptc (Ingham et al., 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: During its movement, Hh forms a gradient of decreasing concentration with increasing distance from the a/p border which corresponds to differential activation of different Hh target genes.
source: During its movement, Hh forms a gradient of decreasing concentration with increasing distance from the a/p border which corresponds to differential activation of different Hh target genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about morphogen gradients.

claim: Up to ten cell diameters from the a/p boundary, high Hh levels directly pattern the central L3-L4 region of the wing (Mullor et al., 1997; Strigini and Cohen, 1997) by stabilizing Ci155.
source: Up to ten cell diameters from the a/p boundary, high Hh levels directly pattern the central L3-L4 region of the wing (Mullor et al., 1997; Strigini and Cohen, 1997) by stabilizing Ci155.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by two citations.

claim: More distal regions, up to 12–15 cell diameters from the a/p border, depend on Dpp, which is secreted in a stripe just anterior to the a/p boundary in response to low Hh levels.
source: More distal regions, up to 12–15 cell diameters from the a/p border, depend on Dpp, which is secreted in a stripe just anterior to the a/p boundary in response to low Hh levels.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Hh-dependent patterning.

claim: En-regulated overexpression of Hh (en >Hh) expanded the L3-L4 intervein area.
source: As previously shown (Crozatier et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2001; Mullor et al., 1997; Strigini and Cohen, 1997), en >Hh expanded the L3-L4 intervein area and, as a concomitant effect, reduced the L2-L3 intervein space (Figure 2c).

source: By contrast, en-regulated overexpression of non-palmitoylated, biologically inactive HhC85S (en >HhC85S) resulted in L3-L4 veins being proximally apposed and the formation of ectopic anterior cross veins (Figure 2d) (Crozatier et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2001)
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, consistent with previous work cited, and shown in Figure 2d.

claim: HhC85S competes with bioactive wild-type Hh (Lee et al., 2001).
source: suggesting that HhC85S competes with bioactive wild-type Hh (Lee et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: En >Hh expression resulted in L3-L4/L2-L3 ratio of 0.108 ± 0.005 (+46% compared to control), p<0.0001.
source: en >GFP served as a normal control: L3-L4/L2-L3 = 0.074 ± 0.002; en >Hh = 0.108 ± 0.005 (+46%), p<0.0001

claim: En >HhC85S expression resulted in L3-L4/L2-L3 ratio of 0.032 ± 0.002 (-57% compared to control), p<0.0001.
evidence: This is quantitative data from the current study shown in Figure 2e,f.

source: Indeed, HhC85S expression under ptc control had little effect on wing development (Figure 2g,h: ptc >GFP: 0.084 ± 0.001, ptc >HhC85S: 0.078 ± 0.002 (-7%), p=0.0026)

source: suggesting that HhC85S cell-autonomously interferes with endogenous Hh, possibly by the random mixing of inactive HhC85S and wild-type Hh at the cell surface (Figure 2i, left).

source: In this mixed association, unprocessed HhC85S N-terminal peptides block wild-type Hh-receptor-binding sites in trans.

claim: Ptc>HhC85S expression in the anterior compartment prevents mixed cluster formation and therefore does not affect the controlled secretion and signaling of endogenous Hh.
source: By contrast, ptc>HhC85S expression in the anterior compartment prevents mixed cluster formation and therefore does not affect the controlled secretion and signaling of endogenous Hh (Figure 2i, right).

claim: Expression of soluble HhNC85S under en-control did not affect endogenous Hh function in vivo.
source: We observed that the expression of soluble HhNC85S under en-control did not affect endogenous Hh function in vivo (Figure 3b)

claim: En >HhNC85S expression did not significantly affect wing development (en >HhNC85S (1): 0.07 ± 0.001 (-5%) (p=0.0707), en >HhNC85S (2): 0.074 ± 0.001 (±0%) (p=0.9419), en >HhNC85S (3): 0.075 ± 0.002 (+1%) (p=0.6050)).
source: relative L3-L4/L2-L3 ratios obtained from three independent HhNC85S lines (1-3) revealed that wing development was not significantly affected (en >GFP: 0.074 ± 0.002, en >HhNC85S (1): 0.07 ± 0.001 (-5%) (p=0.0707), en >HhNC85S (2): 0.074 ± 0.001 (±0%) (p=0.9419), en >HhNC85S (3): 0.075 ± 0.002 (+1%) (p=0.6050), 20 wings were quantified in each line).

claim: HhNC85S expression under ptc control resulted in a small, yet significant gain-of-function phenotype (ptc >HhNC85S (1): 0.091 ± 0.002 (+8%) (p=0.0013), ptc >HhNC85S (2): 0.089 ± 0.002 (+6%) (p=0.0348), ptc >HhNC85S (3): 0.093 ± 0.001 (+11%) (p<0.0001)).
source: Notably, HhNC85S expression under ptc control resulted in a small, yet significant gain-of-function phenotype (Figure 3d,e, ptc >GFP: 0.084 ± 0.001, ptc >HhNC85S (1): 0.091 ± 0.002 (+8%) (p=0.0013), ptc >HhNC85S (2): 0.089 ± 0.002 (+6%) (p=0.0348), ptc >HhNC85S (3): 0.093 ± 0.001 (+11%) (p<0.0001), 20 wings were quantified in each line).

claim: Hh inactivation by adjacent unprocessed N-terminal peptides in trans is restricted to clustered, but not unclustered proteins (Ohlig et al., 2011; Ohlig et al., 2012).
source: This is consistent with the concept that Hh inactivation by adjacent unprocessed N-terminal peptides in trans is restricted to clustered, but not unclustered proteins (Ohlig et al., 2011; Ohlig et al., 2012).

claim: Multimeric HhC85S eluted in gel filtration fractions 3–8, corresponding to molecular weights of 70 kDa-600 kDa.

source: These results are consistent with the assembly of Hh clusters by direct protein-protein contacts as a prerequisite for the inhibitory activity of unprocessed N-terminal peptides.

claim: Hh concentrations at any position in the gradient will strictly correlate with their biological activities (i.e. their Ptc-binding capacities).

claim: N-palmitate controls Hh release from the cell surface in vitro.

claim: Dual-lipidated Shh and ShhHA yielded strong cellular signals but were absent from media, indicating impaired release.

claim: Non-palmitoylated ShhC25S;HA was effectively converted into a C-terminally truncated soluble morphogen.

claim: N-palmitoylation controls protein solubilization in vitro (1 hr release: ShhC25A 94 ± 3 a.u., ShhNC25A 265 ± 10 a.u., p<0.0001, n = 3; 4 hr release: Shh 18 ± 2 a.u., ShhC25A 238 ± 6 a.u., p>0.0001, n = 3, ShhNC25A 500 ± 58 a.u., p>0.001, n = 2).

claim: Only low levels of HAHh that retained the tag were solubilized, suggesting that N-terminal processing was impaired in S2 cells.

claim: N-palmitoylation controls Hh release from the cell surface and restricts possible modes of Hh solubilization to shedding.

evidence: This is a conclusion from the current study based on experimental data illustrated in Figure 6f,g.

claim: HAHh expression in the posterior compartment at 25°C largely arrested fly development at the pupal and pharate stages, leading to defective head development characteristic of Hh loss of function (Torroja et al., 2004).
source: Indeed, HAHh expression in the posterior compartment at 25°C largely arrested fly development at the pupal and pharate stages, leading to defective head development characteristic of Hh loss of function (Torroja et al., 2004).

source: Of 230 pharates counted, only three imagos hatched with smaller wings lacking anterior structures (Figure 7b), again characteristic of Hh loss of function (Bejarano et al., 2012).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the current study shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Reduced transgene expression at 18°C largely reversed pharate lethality: 77% of en> HAHh pharates hatched (293 flies from 393 pupae).
source: Reduced transgene expression at 18°C largely reversed pharate lethality: 77% of en> HAHh pharates hatched (293 flies from 393 pupae)
evidence: This is quantitative data from the current study.

claim: All analyzed en> HAHh wings at 18°C lacked all or most of the L3-L4 intervein area.
source: but wing development was still impaired with all analyzed wings lacking all or most of the L3-L4 intervein area (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 7c.

claim: HAHh expression under ptc-control showed only minor effects.
source: Notably, the observation that HAHh expression under ptc-control showed only minor effects (Figure 7h,i) confirms cell-autonomous Hh repression by direct HAHh contacts in mixed clusters
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 7h,i.

claim: Palmitoylated HAHh peptides restrain mixed Hh/HAHh clusters at the cell membrane.
source: and suggests that palmitoylated HAHh peptides restrain these mixed clusters at the cell membrane.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Additional C > S mutagenesis in HAHhC85S fully reversed pharate lethality at 25°C and led to wing phenotypes comparable to those of en >HhC85S flies.
source: Indeed, additional mutagenesis of the palmitate acceptor cysteine in en >HAHhC85S flies fully reversed pharate lethality at 25°C and led to wing phenotypes comparable to those of en >HhC85S flies (compare Figure 7d with 7 f and Figure 7e with 7 g).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 7d-g.

claim: Posterior Hh overexpression expanded dpp-LacZ expression anteriorly.
source: We confirmed that posterior Hh overexpression expanded dpp-LacZ expression anteriorly (Figure 8c)
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 8c.

claim: Posterior Hh overexpression expanded ptc-LacZ expression in the presumptive L3-L4 region.
source: and, consistent with established en >Hh expansion of the L3-L4 intervein area (Figure 2c), we confirmed that posterior Hh overexpression expanded ptc-LacZ expression in the presumptive L3-L4 region (Figure 8d).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 8d.

claim: En-controlled expression of HAHh at 18°C did not much affect dpp-LacZ expression in the anterior compartment.
source: En-controlled expression of the HA-tagged protein at 18°C, in contrast, did not much affect dpp-LacZ expression in the anterior compartment (Figure 8e)
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 8e.

claim: En-controlled expression of HAHh at 18°C abolished all ptc-LacZ reporter expression and restricted en-expression posteriorly.
source: but abolished all ptc-LacZ reporter expression and restricted en-expression posteriorly (Figure 8f).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 8f.

claim: The complete loss of L3-L4 intervein tissue in adult en >HAHh wings is caused by insufficient Hh levels at the a/p border.
source: This confirms that the complete loss of L3-L4 intervein tissue in adult en >HAHh wings is caused by insufficient Hh levels at the a/p border
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Coexpressed HAHh impaired Hh release from the posterior compartment of the wing disc.
source: and supports the idea that coexpressed HAHh impaired Hh release from the posterior compartment of the wing disc.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: The observed expansion of dpp expression can be best explained by abrogated Ptc-mediated Hh internalization that normally restricts the Hh gradient (Chen and Struhl, 1996).
source: We note that the observed expansion of dpp expression can be best explained by abrogated Ptc-mediated Hh internalization that normally restricts the Hh gradient (Chen and Struhl, 1996).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: HAHhC85S coexpression restored ptc-LacZ and dpp-LacZ expression to levels comparable to those detected in HhC85S expressing wing discs.
source: Consistent with our concept of N-palmitate serving as a membrane anchor to prevent unregulated Hh release, HAHhC85S coexpression restored ptc-LacZ and dpp-LacZ expression (Figure 8g,h) to levels comparable to those detected in HhC85S expressing wing discs (Figure 8i,j)
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 8g-j.

claim: Additional deletion of the unpalmitoylated N-terminal peptide reverted the expanded area of dpp-LacZ expression to wild-type range.
source: and additional deletion of the unpalmitoylated N-terminal peptide reverted the expanded area of dpp-LacZ expression to wild-type range (Figure 8k,l).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 8k,l.

claim: N-terminal Hh processing converts the insoluble Hh cluster into truncated, bioactive morphogen.
source: Together, these experiments confirm that N-terminal Hh processing converts the insoluble Hh cluster into truncated, bioactive morphogen
evidence: This is a conclusion from the current study based on experimental evidence.

claim: The palmitate anchor controls completion of N-terminal Hh processing.
source: and that the palmitate anchor controls completion of this process.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the current study based on experimental evidence.

claim: Targeted coexpression of Hh and HAHhC85S fully reverted dominant-negative HAHhC85S function in 80% of wings and expanded the L3-L4 intervein area in the remaining 20% of wings.
source: Targeted coexpression of both proteins fully reverted dominant-negative HAHhC85S function in 80% of wings and expanded this area in the remaining 20% of wings (56 wings were analyzed, Figure 9c,d).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the current study shown in Figure 9c,d.

claim: Increased Hh amounts 'titer out' dominant-negative HAHhC85S function.
source: This indicates that increased Hh amounts 'titer out' dominant-negative HAHhC85S function.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: En >Hh did not significantly correct dominant-negative HAHh mis-patterning phenotypes.
source: In contrast, en >Hh did not significantly correct dominant-negative HAHh mis-patterning phenotypes.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: HAHh expression in the posterior compartment arrested fly development at pupal and pharate stages, with all wings of about 4% imagos that hatched (n = 12/320) lacking most anterior structures.
source: As previously shown, HAHh expression in the posterior compartment arrested fly development at pupal and pharate stages. All wings of about 4% imagos that hatched (n = 12/320) lacked most anterior structures (Figure 9d,e).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the current study shown in Figure 9d,e.

claim: Hh coexpression with HAHh partially reversed pharate lethality (22% imagos hatched, n = 41/182), but all analyzed wings still lacked the complete L3-L4 intervein area.
source: Hh coexpression partially reversed pharate lethality (22% imagos hatched, n = 41/182), but all analyzed wings still lacked the complete L3-L4 intervein area (Figure 9d,f).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the current study shown in Figure 9d,f.

claim: Increased relative Hh amounts 'dilute' the average number of permanent membrane anchors of any given mixed cluster, with only a limited compensatory effect on Hh release and activity due to the remaining tethers.
source: The most likely explanation for this is that increased relative Hh amounts 'dilute' the average number of permanent membrane anchors of any given mixed cluster, with only a limited compensatory effect on Hh release and activity due to the remaining tethers.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: 34B > Hh expression at 25°C led to clear anterior overgrowth in 90% of wings.
source: 34B > Hh expression at 25°C led to clear anterior overgrowth in 90% of wings.
evidence: This is quantitative data from the current study shown in Figure 9g.

claim: 34B > HAHhC85S or HAHh expression did not impair wing development.
source: 34B > HAHhCC85S or HAHh expression did not impair wing development. This again confirmed biological inactivity of both Hh variants.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 9h,i.

claim: 34B-controlled Hh;HAHhC85S coexpression partially reversed Hh gain-of-function, reducing ectopic overgrowth to a small fraction of wings (8%).
source: 34B-controlled Hh;HAHhC85S coexpression partially reversed Hh gain-of-function, reducing ectopic overgrowth to a small fraction of wings (8%).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the current study shown in Figure 9j,l.

claim: 34B > Hh;HAHh coexpression completely reversed Hh gain-of-function.
source: 34B > Hh;HAHh coexpression completely reversed Hh gain-of-function. This confirms cell-autonomous Hh repression by direct HAHh contacts in mixed clusters, as quantified in (l).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 9k,l.

claim: Coexpressed Hh fully restored dominant-negative HAHhC85S function by expanding ptc-LacZ target gene expression in the presumptive L3-L4 region in the anterior compartment.
source: Consistent with the restored formation of L3-L4 intervein tissue in adult en >Hh;HAHhC85S wings (Figure 9c), and occasionally gain-of-function in these wings, ptc-LacZ expression in the anterior compartment of the wing disc was expanded (Figure 10d). This shows that coexpressed Hh fully restored dominant-negative HAHhC85S function by expanding ptc-LacZ target gene expression in the presumptive L3-L4 region in the anterior compartment
evidence: This is a finding from the current study shown in Figure 10d.

claim: Receiving cells respond to the morphogen when Hh is coexpressed with HAHhC85S.
source: and demonstrates that receiving cells respond to the morphogen.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the current study based on experimental evidence.

claim: A significant fraction of Hh assembles into extended linear arrays at the cell surface.
source: Here, we provide ultrastructural data showing that a significant fraction of Hh assembles into extended linear arrays
evidence: This is a conclusion from the current study based on IEM data.

claim: Linear Hh assembly is consistent with the long unbranched HS-chain structure that scaffolds Hh clusters (Vyas et al., 2008), observed crystal lattice interactions of the vertebrate Shh ortholog (Pepinsky et al., 1998) and functional in vitro data (Ohlig et al., 2011; Ohlig et al., 2012).
source: consistent with the long unbranched HS-chain structure that scaffolds Hh clusters (Vyas et al., 2008), observed crystal lattice interactions of the vertebrate Shh ortholog (Pepinsky et al., 1998) and functional in vitro data (Ohlig et al., 2011; Ohlig et al., 2012).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Expression of N-truncated Hh mutants in Drosophila revealed that inhibitory peptide removal unmasks Ptc-binding sites and mediates direct, high threshold tissue patterning (Strigini and Cohen, 1997).
source: Consistent with this, expression of N-truncated Hh mutants in Drosophila revealed that inhibitory peptide removal unmasks Ptc-binding sites and mediates direct, high threshold tissue patterning (Strigini and Cohen, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: All artificially truncated HhC85S;Δ variants were functionally inert.
source: Yet, contrary to previous observations on N-truncated Shh (Ohlig et al., 2011), we note that all artificially truncated HhC85S;Δ variants were functionally inert.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: HhC85S;Δ inactivity may be due to misfolding caused by possible intramolecular chaperone function of the 84 amino acid N-terminal Hh pre-peptide (Eder and Fersht, 1995) or unproductive Ptc binding of artificially truncated proteins as described for monomeric ShhN (Williams et al., 1999).
source: We explain this inactivity by HhC85S;Δ misfolding due to possible intramolecular chaperone function of the 84 amino acid N-terminal Hh pre-peptide (Eder and Fersht, 1995) or unproductive Ptc binding of artificially truncated proteins as described for monomeric ShhN (Williams et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations.

claim: Proteolytic conversion targets the N-terminal CW-site in vitro (Dierker et al., 2009; Ohlig et al., 2012).
source: We previously showed that proteolytic conversion targets the N-terminal CW-site in vitro (Dierker et al., 2009; Ohlig et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citations.

claim: Insertion of HA peptides, which displaces the CW cleavage site distally without affecting Hh N-palmitoylation (Hardy and Resh, 2012) and HS-dependent multimerization, is sufficient to impair endogenous and transgenic Hh high threshold biofunction in vivo, apparently without affecting low threshold Dpp-mediated Hh activity.
source: We show here that insertion of HA peptides, which displaces this cleavage site distally without affecting Hh N-palmitoylation (Hardy and Resh, 2012) and HS-dependent multimerization, is sufficient to impair endogenous and transgenic Hh high threshold biofunction in vivo, apparently without affecting low threshold Dpp-mediated Hh activity.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, with one aspect supported by a citation.

claim: Rescue of Hh biofunction by the additional mutation of the cysteine acceptor shows that N-palmitate anchors the unprocessed peptide to the cell membrane to safeguard Hh release.
source: Rescue of Hh biofunction by the additional mutation of the cysteine acceptor shows that N-palmitate anchors the unprocessed peptide to the cell membrane to safeguard Hh release.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the current study based on experimental evidence.

claim: These findings are consistent with enhanced Drosophila Hh release upon RNAi-mediated knockdown of Hh acyltransferase activity (Chamoun et al., 2001) and increased Shh tethering to cell membranes by palmitate (Konitsiotis et al., 2014; Levental et al., 2010).
source: These findings are consistent with enhanced Drosophila Hh release upon RNAi-mediated knockdown of Hh acyltransferase activity (Chamoun et al., 2001) and increased Shh tethering to cell membranes by palmitate (Konitsiotis et al., 2014; Levental et al., 2010).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Amide-linked Hh palmitate is thioesterase resistant.
source: Importantly, while S- and O-linked palmitate moieties are susceptible to enzymatic deacylation by palmitoyl-protein thioesterases (Kakugawa et al., 2015), amide-linked Hh palmitate is thioesterase resistant.
evidence: This is established knowledge, with the first part supported by a citation.

claim: Hh relay from posterior subcellular structures requires proteolytic processing of sheddase-accessible, membrane-proximal terminal target peptides.
source: This suggests that Hh relay from posterior subcellular structures – at least at some point – requires proteolytic processing of sheddase-accessible, membrane-proximal terminal target peptides.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the current study based on experimental evidence.

claim: Replacement of the C-terminal Hh target peptide with transmembrane-CD2 results in Hh-CD2 fusion proteins that remain permanently membrane associated and generate wings with one single central vein in the region normally occupied by veins L3 and L4, while leaving Dpp-mediated anterior and posterior wing patterning intact (Strigini and Cohen, 1997).
source: Support for this idea comes from the published replacement of the C-terminal Hh target peptide with transmembrane-CD2 (Strigini and Cohen, 1997). Resulting Hh-CD2 fusion proteins remain permanently membrane associated and generate wings with one single central vein in the region normally occupied by veins L3 and L4, while leaving Dpp-mediated anterior and posterior wing patterning intact.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The Hh-CD2 phenotype is strikingly similar to the en >HAHh phenotype.
source: We note that this phenotype is strikingly similar to the en >HAHh phenotype described here.
evidence: This is a comparison made in the current study.

claim: Required Hh transfer between protruding cell-cell contact structures emanating from the Hh-sending and Hh-receiving compartments, called cytonemes, was recently indicated by impaired Ptc signaling and internalization at contact sites with Hh-CD2 (González-Méndez et al., 2017).
source: Moreover, required Hh transfer between protruding cell-cell contact structures emanating from the Hh-sending and Hh-receiving compartments, called cytonemes, was recently indicated by impaired Ptc signaling and internalization at contact sites with Hh-CD2 (González-Méndez et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Proteolytic Hh relay and reception at cytoneme contact sites was suggested by González-Méndez et al., 2017, and is supported by the results shown in this work.
source: While the exact mechanism by which Hh is liberated from the posterior cytoneme membrane was not addressed, proteolytic Hh relay and reception at cytoneme contact sites was suggested by the authors, and is supported by the results shown in our work (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the current study, supported by previous work and data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The Hh gradient in Drosophila wing imaginal discs consists of apical and basolateral secreted pools formed as a consequence of initial apical Hh secretion, subsequent reinternalization, and apical (D'Angelo et al., 2015) or basolateral (Callejo et al., 2011) resecretion, both depending on the endosomal sorting complex required for transport (ESCRT).
source: It has been suggested that the Hh gradient in Drosophila wing imaginal discs consists of apical and basolateral secreted pools formed as a consequence of initial apical Hh secretion, subsequent reinternalization, and apical (D'Angelo et al., 2015) or basolateral (Callejo et al., 2011) resecretion, both depending on the endosomal sorting complex required for transport (ESCRT).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Pools of Hh and ESCRT proteins are secreted together into the extracellular space (Gradilla et al., 2014; Matusek et al., 2014; Vyas et al., 2014).
source: Pools of Hh and ESCRT proteins are then secreted together into the extracellular space (Gradilla et al., 2014; Matusek et al., 2014; Vyas et al., 2014)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Hh is transported on (Bischoff et al., 2013) or inside of (Chen et al., 2017) basolateral cytonemes.
source: Hh being transported on (Bischoff et al., 2013) or inside of (Chen et al., 2017) basolateral cytonemes
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Hh is apically released to promote Hh long-range activity (Ayers et al., 2010).
source: or apically released to promote Hh long-range activity (Ayers et al., 2010) (Figure 12).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 12.

claim: Timely and reliable paracrine Hh function through proteolytic release and extracellular apical diffusion alone is difficult to envision for two reasons: patterning of folded epithelia poses a problem if spreading were to occur out of the plane of the epithelial cell layer through diffusion or flow, and it normally takes much time for diffusing molecules to travel long distances away from the source because the timescale of diffusion increases with the square of the distance (Berg, 1993; Müller and Schier, 2011).
source: While Hh shedding may target several of these pools, timely and reliable paracrine Hh function through proteolytic release and extracellular apical diffusion alone (Figure 12b'') is difficult to envision for two reasons. First, patterning of folded epithelia, such as the Drosophila imaginal disc, poses a problem if spreading were to occur out of the plane of the epithelial cell layer through diffusion or flow, as this would result in morphogen loss into the peripodial space and loss of long-range Hh function. The second limitation is that it normally takes much time for diffusing molecules to travel long distances away from the source because the timescale of diffusion increases with the square of the distance (Berg, 1993; Müller and Schier, 2011).
evidence: This is a theoretical argument supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 12.

claim: Cytoneme- or exosome-mediated basolateral transport, followed by proteolytic Hh relay over short distances at membrane contact sites (González-Méndez et al., 2017), would effectively solve both problems of morphogen spreading in folded epithelia.
source: Cytoneme- or exosome-mediated basolateral transport, followed by proteolytic Hh relay over short distances at membrane contact sites (González-Méndez et al., 2017), would effectively solve both problems
evidence: This is a proposed solution supported by a citation.

claim: Heparan sulfate proteoglycan 'restricted' Hh transport at the apical cell surface (Han et al., 2004) would solve the problems of morphogen spreading in folded epithelia.
source: as would the idea of heparan sulfate proteoglycan 'restricted' Hh transport at the apical cell surface (Han et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a proposed alternative solution supported by a citation.

claim: Shifted is a soluble protein with structural similarities to vertebrate Scube2 sheddase enhancers (Jakobs et al., 2014; Jakobs et al., 2016; Jakobs et al., 2017).
source: We also aim to characterize the Hh release factor Shifted (Glise et al., 2005), a soluble protein with structural similarities to vertebrate Scube2 sheddase enhancers (Jakobs et al., 2014; Jakobs et al., 2016; Jakobs et al., 2017)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Palmitate-controlled quantitative Hh shedding from the cell surface constitutes an essential step in Hh transmission and high-threshold tissue patterning in vivo.
source: In conclusion, we propose that palmitate-controlled quantitative Hh shedding from the cell surface constitutes an essential step in Hh transmission and high-threshold tissue patterning in vivo.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the current study.

claim: The results on Hh processing and palmitate function are expected to be relevant to other Hh-dependent developmental programs and to Hh ligand-dependent cancer induction and progression (Amakye et al., 2013).
source: While we have used Drosophila wing development to elucidate this molecular process, we expect our results to also be relevant to other Hh-dependent developmental programs and to Hh ligand-dependent cancer induction and progression (Amakye et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader relevance of the findings, with cancer relevance supported by a citation.
